title: Preface
summary: NVIDIA Corporation’s Form 10-K covers the fiscal year ended January 28, 2024, and identifies its incorporation, headquarters, tax ID, listed common stock, filing status, filer classification, internal-control attestation, market value, and shares outstanding. It incorporates proxy-statement material into Part III. The contents list Parts I–IV: business, risks and other disclosures; market information, management analysis and financial statements; governance, compensation and related-party matters; and exhibits, financial schedules and a Form 10-K summary.

title: Where You Can Find More Information
summary: NVIDIA discloses material information through its investor relations website, press releases, SEC filings, public calls and webcasts, and social media channels (X, corporate blog, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram), with YouTube hosting videos. Social posts may be material and support Regulation FD compliance, so investors should monitor them alongside traditional channels. The channel list may change and is available on NVIDIA’s investor relations website; these channels’ content is not part of the Annual Report on Form 10-K.

title: Forward-Looking Statements
summary: The report defines forward-looking statements and identifying terms, warns that risks and uncertainties may cause actual outcomes to differ, points readers to Risk Factors, and cautions against undue reliance. Statements reflect estimates and information available only as of the filing date; NVIDIA generally has no duty to update them except as required by law. “NVIDIA,” “we,” “us,” “our,” and “Company” refer to NVIDIA Corporation and its subsidiaries. “We believe” statements reflect opinions based on potentially limited information, not exhaustive review, and are also uncertain.

title: Item 1. Business Our Company

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Our Company (intro)
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its evolution into a full-stack accelerated-computing company, combining GPUs, CUDA, software, networking, and data-center-scale systems for AI, analytics, scientific computing, graphics, and industry-specific applications. It explains GPU and AI uses, its platform and developer ecosystem, and innovation milestones from the GPU and CUDA to Tensor Cores, Mellanox networking, software stacks, and Grace CPU. It serves cloud providers, enterprises, researchers, gamers, and creative professionals, and gives its history, two reporting segments (Compute & Networking and Graphics), and four major markets. The Data Center section details its compute and networking products, deployment environments, customers, and partners.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Businesses, Markets, and Applications
nodes.summary: NVIDIA computing supports scientific research, TOP500 supercomputers, gaming and creative work, and growing local and enterprise generative AI uses. Founded in California in 1993 and reincorporated in Delaware in 1998, NVIDIA reports two segments: Compute & Networking (data center, networking, automotive, robotics, AI software, and DGX Cloud) and Graphics (gaming, workstations, streaming, virtual GPUs, automotive infotainment, and Omniverse). Its integrated computing platforms serve four key markets: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.

nodes.title: Data Center
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s data center platform accelerates AI, analytics, graphics, and scientific computing through integrated GPUs, DPUs, CPUs, networking, software, and services for cloud, enterprise, and edge customers. Its offerings include InfiniBand and Ethernet systems, CUDA and AI software, enterprise licenses, and DGX Cloud; the data center is increasingly the computing unit for large-scale workloads. The text also covers gaming GPUs, cloud gaming, RTX ray tracing and DLSS; professional visualization, RTX workflows, and Omniverse digital twins and simulations; and automotive platforms for autonomous driving and in-vehicle computing.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Computing Platforms and Market Solutions
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its GPU-based accelerated computing platform, expanded with DPUs and CPUs, its software ecosystem, paid AI and virtualization software, and DGX Cloud. Gaming coverage includes industry growth drivers, RTX ray tracing and DLSS, AI PC capabilities, and GeForce, cloud gaming, and console products. Professional Visualization covers GPU-optimized workflows, RTX real-time rendering, and Omniverse for simulation and industrial digital twins. Automotive focuses on automated-driving and cockpit platforms, including DRIVE Hyperion and AI pilot and co-pilot applications.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its accelerated-computing platform: GPUs, expanded with DPUs and CPUs, are optimized across computing, networking, and storage and supported by CUDA, CUDA-X, frameworks, paid AI Enterprise and vGPU software, and DGX Cloud AI training services. Gaming offerings use RTX ray tracing and DLSS, alongside GeForce GPUs, cloud gaming, and console technology. Professional Visualization serves design and content-creation workflows with RTX and Omniverse for industrial digital twins and simulation. Automotive solutions include DRIVE Hyperion hardware, sensors, software, partner-developed autonomous-driving systems, DRIVE Sim, cockpit computing, and ongoing over-the-air updates.

nodes.title: Business Strategies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s strategy centers on advancing its unified accelerated-computing platform; extending leadership in AI, graphics, and autonomous vehicles; and licensing or custom-developing its IP. Its AI offering spans hardware, networking, software, cloud services, developer tools, and education, supported by a broad ecosystem. Graphics technologies serve gaming, creative work, simulation, and cloud access; DRIVE targets AVs and EVs. Sales teams and partners provide technical support and foster software development. Gaming revenue is typically stronger in the fiscal year’s second half, though this may vary. Fabless manufacturing relies on suppliers for production, with supply-chain concentration in Asia-Pacific and efforts to build capacity, redundancy, and resilience.

nodes.title: Sales, Seasonality, and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The page describes an end-to-end autonomous-driving solution, including neural-network training hardware and intellectual-property licensing and development agreements. It outlines global sales and marketing through partners, technical pre-sales support, developer engagement, and training programs. Gaming revenue typically strengthens in the fiscal year’s second half, though trends may vary. Manufacturing is fabless and outsourced to certified suppliers; the company may secure components and capacity in advance, and has expanded supplier redundancy. Its supply chain is concentrated in Asia-Pacific, with named providers for wafers, memory, packaging, assembly, testing, and final products.

nodes.title: Competition and Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The page describes intense, evolving competition in accelerated computing and networking, key competitive factors, expected new entrants and market pressures, and competitors across GPUs, CPUs, AI/cloud platforms, SoCs, and networking. It also outlines IP protections through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, agreements, licenses, and international laws; patent coverage and expiration dates; weaker protections and piracy risks in some countries; criteria for pursuing formal protection; and ongoing third-party technology licensing.

nodes.title: Regulatory Risks and Sustainability Governance
nodes.summary: The page describes U.S. export licensing restrictions on NVIDIA products, especially advanced chips and systems destined for China, Russia, and other regions, and their potential effects on sales, competitiveness, inventory, product development, and Asia-Pacific-focused supply chains. It also notes broader regulatory compliance risks and currently limited material effects or anticipated environmental-control spending. NVIDIA outlines its sustainability and governance goals, board oversight, annual program assessments, stakeholder priorities, and related reporting and risk disclosures.

nodes.title: Climate Change
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes climate efforts across its product lifecycle, regulatory risk assessment, FY2023 impact metrics and planned FY2024 reporting, renewable-electricity targets and progress, supplier emissions engagement, energy-efficient GPU computing, and its planned Earth-2 climate digital twin. It also outlines human-capital oversight, workforce size and composition, recruiting and diversity efforts, employee development and feedback channels, low turnover, performance-linked compensation and equity, and global health, financial, family, and well-being benefits.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Sustainability and Human Capital
nodes.summary: NVIDIA reports renewable electricity progress and supplier emissions-target goals, highlights energy-efficient GPU computing and its Green500 presence, and describes Earth-2 climate modeling plans. It outlines its global workforce and human capital oversight, recruitment and workforce diversity, employee learning, mentoring, career mobility and feedback channels, and a 2.7% fiscal 2024 turnover rate.

nodes.title: Compensation, Benefits, and Well-Being
nodes.summary: The text describes performance-based compensation, time-vested equity, global health, retirement, stock-purchase, flexible-work and leave benefits, tailored family and crisis support; diversity and inclusion recruiting, development, training, monitoring, and workforce representation (fiscal 2024); and flexible work plus quarterly recharge days planned for fiscal 2025. It lists five executives’ ages and roles as of February 16, 2024, then summarizes Jen-Hsun Huang’s and Colette Kress’s careers and education.

nodes.title: Workforce Support, Inclusion, and Flexibility
nodes.summary: The company enhances support for employees and families during crises. It promotes diversity and inclusion through targeted recruiting, partnerships, employee development and resource groups, training, equity tracking, and progress reporting. At fiscal year-end 2024, its global workforce was 79% male, 20% female, and 1% undeclared; 6% of U.S. employees were Black/African American or Hispanic/Latino. Flexible work supports hiring, retention, and engagement, and fiscal 2025 plans include continued flexibility and two company-wide days off per quarter.

nodes.title: Information About Our Executive Officers
nodes.summary: The text lists NVIDIA’s five executive officers, their ages and positions as of February 16, 2024, and summarizes their careers and education. CEO and co-founder Jen-Hsun Huang’s prior semiconductor roles and engineering degrees are described, along with CFO Colette Kress’s finance leadership at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments; Ajay Puri’s sales and management career at NVIDIA, Sun Microsystems and other firms; Debora Shoquist’s operations leadership at NVIDIA and technology companies; and General Counsel Timothy Teter’s NVIDIA role, prior technology litigation practice and engineering and law degrees.

nodes.title: Available Information
nodes.summary: NVIDIA provides free access on its website to its annual, quarterly, and current SEC reports and applicable amendments as soon as reasonably practicable after filing or furnishing them. The SEC website also offers reports, proxy and information statements, and other information about electronic filers. NVIDIA’s website and linked content are not part of its Form 10-K.

summary: NVIDIA’s business, history, reporting segments, and four markets are described, including its integrated GPU-, DPU-, CPU-, networking-, and software-based accelerated-computing platforms and offerings in data centers, gaming, professional visualization, and automotive. The section covers strategy, customers, partners, sales, seasonality, outsourced manufacturing and supply chains, competition, intellectual property, export controls and other regulation, sustainability and climate initiatives, human-capital oversight, workforce composition, inclusion, compensation, benefits and flexibility, executive officers’ backgrounds, and where to access company and SEC filings.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors

nodes.title: Risk Factors: Markets, Demand, and Manufacturing
key_items: Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets
Risks Related to Demand, Supply and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The page warns that disclosed and currently unknown or seemingly immaterial risks may harm the company’s business, financial condition, results, or reputation and lower its stock price. Risks include failing to meet evolving industry needs, competition, inaccurate demand estimates causing supply mismatches, reliance on third-party suppliers and technology limiting control over product quantity, quality, yields, and delivery, and product defects leading to remediation costs and business damage.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Global Operating Business
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks to the company’s global business, including economic downturns; international operations; cyberattacks, data breaches and business disruptions; climate change; unsuccessful investments, acquisitions or integration; reliance on key partners, distributors and customers; employee retention; information-system and internal-control interruptions; and fluctuating results and stock price. It also covers regulatory, legal and corporate risks: complex laws and political actions; sustainability scrutiny; responsible technology and AI use; intellectual property; privacy and security obligations; taxes; litigation and investigations; debt; and provisions that could delay or prevent a change in control.

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Rapid technological, customer, competitive, and standards changes make success depend on adapting strategy; developing or acquiring products through R&D; launching software, services, and cloud offerings; expanding ecosystems; meeting safety, security, reliability, and compliance expectations; managing product lifecycles; scaling and securing infrastructure, energy, and operational capabilities; and funding required investments. R&D in unfamiliar markets may yield little or delayed revenue; products may not be adopted or valued, and lengthy design-win processes offer no revenue guarantee and can affect future wins. DGX Cloud and other standalone software offerings require substantial time and investment, face changing availability and timelines, and may fail to generate meaningful revenue.

nodes.title: Competition could adversely impact our market share and financial results.
nodes.summary: Intensifying competition from changing offerings, standards, customer needs, new entrants, and consolidation could reduce our market share and financial results. Competitors may offer cheaper or better products and have advantages in fabrication, experience, customers, intellectual property, design wins, and resources, enabling them to capture markets, pursue trends, transition products faster, and secure scarce manufacturing capacity and materials. Customers may replace our solutions with in-house or competing services, including cloud-based AI offerings. Failure to compete or achieve sufficient scale could reduce demand and prevent meaningful revenue.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply and Manufacturing Failure to estimate customer demand accurately has led and could lead to mismatches between supply and demand.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from inaccurate demand forecasting amid outsourced manufacturing, long and uncertain lead times, limited capacity, and supply-chain complexity. Demand shifts, shortages, excess inventory, product transitions, channel estimates, new AI/CPU use cases, cryptocurrency mining, gray markets, geopolitics, and external disruptions can affect supply, revenue, costs, margins, customer relationships, and market share. NVIDIA discusses its fiscal 2024 demand surge, expanded supplier commitments, expected constraints on next-generation products, and potential inventory write-downs. It also depends on third parties to develop applications and provide platform content.

nodes.title: Dependency on third-party suppliers and their technology to manufacture, assemble, test, or package our products reduces our control over product quantity and quality, manufacturing yields, and product delivery schedules and could harm our business.
nodes.summary: Reliance on third-party foundries and subcontractors for wafer fabrication, component procurement, assembly, testing, and packaging limits control over supply, quality, yields, and delivery, potentially harming demand, operations, margins, revenue, and financial results. Risks include inaccurate demand forecasts and insufficient or costly supply; inadequate materials or capacity; process-technology failures; regulatory noncompliance; concentrated suppliers; replacement delays and costs; unqualified product changes; suppliers prioritizing others; noncancelable orders or advance payments; design or process-related low yields; and natural-disaster or power-conservation disruptions.

nodes.title: Defects in our products have caused and could cause us to incur significant expenses to remediate, which can damage our reputation and cause us to lose market share.
nodes.summary: Complex hardware, software, services, and AI offerings may contain defects, vulnerabilities, bias, or performance failures, especially as products evolve and reliance on partners limits production control. Issues may emerge after shipment, expose data or customers to attacks, damage integrated products, and trigger warranty, repair, recall, replacement, inventory write-off, reimbursement, indemnity, or regulatory costs. Remediation may be delayed or unsatisfactory, harming market acceptance, design wins, customer and partner relationships, brand, revenue, margins, and finances. A third-party component defect in fiscal 2023 Data Center products increased costs and led to a warranty liability that may require adjustment. Product liability claims can be costly, divert personnel, and exceed insurance coverage or face unavailable coverage.

nodes.title: Adverse economic conditions may harm our business.
nodes.summary: Economic, industry, geopolitical, and financial uncertainty—including inflation, policy changes, market disruptions, supply constraints, and weaker demand—may raise costs and reduce margins; disrupt suppliers, customers, and partners; limit forecasting and investment; cause insolvencies, reduced customer profitability, competitive changes, credit and collection risks, and lower liquidity or access to capital. Financial-institution instability could impair payment and contractual obligations. The company’s investment portfolio, largely U.S. government securities, faces credit, liquidity, market, and interest-rate risks; prolonged market declines or a U.S. government credit downgrade or default could reduce investment values and liquidity, increase rates, weaken the dollar, and cause investment losses or impairment charges.

nodes.title: International sales and operations are a significant part of our business, which exposes us to risks that could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company’s international sales, operations, and outsourced semiconductor manufacturing expose it to material business, financial, and operational risks. In fiscal 2024, 56% of revenue came from outside the U.S.; China’s share of Data Center revenue fell from 19% in fiscal 2023 to 14% in fiscal 2024, reaching a mid-single-digit share in the fourth quarter and expected to remain similar in fiscal 2025. Without U.S. licenses for restricted products, the company has begun shipping alternatives to China in small volumes. Risks include economic and political conditions, lockdowns and public-health issues, differing legal and business practices, capital-market disruptions, anti-inflation policies, currency movements, disasters, war, terrorism, and other catastrophes.

nodes.title: Product, system security, and data protection breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue, increase our expenses, and significantly harm our business and reputation.
nodes.summary: Cyberattacks and security, privacy, or data breaches—including ransomware, AI-enabled attacks, insider misconduct, geopolitical threats, software failures, and supply-chain vulnerabilities—could disrupt operations and harm revenue, costs, finances, reputation, and customers. Recovery may be difficult, especially if backups are compromised. Third-party systems and datasets create risks that are hard to monitor or investigate; compromised products could affect many customers. Preventing and remediating threats requires ongoing investment, training, and compliance, yet vulnerabilities may go undetected or fixes be delayed. Incidents involving confidential, personal, proprietary, or partner data could cause misuse, litigation, regulatory action, notification duties, disclosure, operational and supply disruptions, lost sales, and other liabilities; sensitive information may also be inferred from public or commercial sources.

nodes.title: Business disruptions could harm our operations, lead to a decline in revenue and increase our costs.
nodes.summary: Disasters, extreme weather, shortages, cyberattacks, supplier or infrastructure failures, conflict, political instability, and regulatory changes could disrupt geographically concentrated operations, suppliers, customers, and third-party services, raising costs and reducing revenue; continuity plans may be inadequate. The company monitors the Israel conflict, which has affected employee support costs and caused military-related absences, though no significant supply-chain or business impact has occurred so far; prolonged conflict could disrupt development, operations, and revenue. Greater reliance on cloud providers and data centers increases exposure to outages and insolvency, while water and energy constraints may limit customers’ capacity and demand.

nodes.title: Climate change may have a long-term impact on our business.
nodes.summary: Climate change may disrupt operations, infrastructure, supply chains, and workforce effectiveness through resource constraints, extreme weather, wildfire-related power shutoffs, and political instability, causing attrition, losses, and recovery costs. Insurance may be costly, limited, or unavailable to cover losses. Climate laws, regulations, lawsuits, and disclosure or supply-chain requirements may raise compliance, energy, capital, and input costs or force operational and product changes. The company also faces reputational, litigation, contractual, and sustainability-goal risks, plus possible customer concern about GPUs’ high absolute energy use despite their relative efficiency.

nodes.title: We may not be able to realize the potential benefits of business investments or acquisitions, and we may not be able to successfully integrate acquired companies, which could hurt our ability to grow our business, develop new products or sell our products.
nodes.summary: Acquisitions and strategic investments may fail to deliver expected benefits, hinder growth, product development or sales, and harm financial results. Risks include delayed or restricted approvals, missed alternatives, lost talent, changing technology, reduced deal value, difficulty completing future deals, illiquid or unsuccessful investments, losses and sector-concentration impairments. Other risks include diverted resources, poor returns, financing or consent barriers, litigation, and inadequate due diligence. Integration may involve technology, systems, operations, employees, accounting, liabilities, debt, equity dilution, variable consideration, economic, cybersecurity, reputational, and relationship risks. Systems integration has caused costly delays, supplier/customer process problems, and training needs that have affected and may continue to affect results.

nodes.title: We receive a significant amount of our revenue from a limited number of partners and distributors and we have a concentration of sales to customers who purchase directly or indirectly from us, and our revenue could be adversely affected if we lose or are prevented from selling to any of these customers.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from revenue concentration among a few customers and channel partners, including purchase changes or cancellations, indirect-customer concentration, quarter-end supply or credit constraints, trade restrictions, and collection difficulties. It covers challenges attracting and retaining key talent, compensation competition, immigration rules, and succession planning. It also warns that business systems and ERP changes could disrupt operations, reporting, and internal controls, with material weaknesses potentially damaging credibility and finances. Finally, results may fluctuate due to spending, contracts, payment terms, vendors, environmental costs, accounting changes, and investment growth; missed expectations could reduce or destabilize the stock price.

nodes.title: Customer, Talent, and Systems Risks
key_items: If we are unable to attract, retain and motivate our executives and key employees, our business may be harmed.

Our business is dependent upon the proper functioning of our business processes and information systems and modification or interruption of such systems may disrupt our business, and internal controls.
nodes.summary: The text warns that customer losses, reduced purchases, trade restrictions, collection difficulties, or constrained channel-partner credit could harm revenue and financial results. It also describes risks from difficulty attracting, retaining, and motivating key employees amid labor competition, cost inflation, immigration rules, compensation volatility, and succession challenges. Reliance on business systems and controls, including ERP implementation, creates disruption, cost, and reporting risks; control weaknesses could undermine investor confidence, require restatements, restrict financing, and trigger regulatory action.

nodes.title: Our operating results have in the past fluctuated and may in the future fluctuate, and if our operating results are below the expectations of securities analysts or investors, our stock price could decline.
nodes.summary: Operating results may fluctuate due to spending flexibility, customer and vendor payment terms, bad debts, environmental costs, accounting changes, and the timing of expenses and investments; disappointing results could reduce stock value. The company also faces extensive global legal and regulatory obligations, investigations, penalties, and changing rules affecting operations, AI, privacy, trade, and other areas. Sanctions and increasingly broad, shifting export controls—especially U.S. restrictions on AI chips and China-related sales—may limit markets, disrupt supply chains and operations, increase costs, delay shipments, disadvantage the company, and reduce demand and revenue. Licensing uncertainty, customer restrictions, geopolitical responses, Chinese policies, and dependence on overseas suppliers, particularly in Taiwan, add further risks.

nodes.title: Increased scrutiny from shareholders, regulators and others regarding our corporate sustainability practices could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from heightened scrutiny of corporate sustainability practices and disclosures, including conflicting regulations, unmet stakeholder expectations, added compliance costs, liability, reputational damage, and lost business. It describes risks from responsible AI use, including social and legal concerns, regulatory costs and restrictions, and harm to adoption, finances, or reputation. It covers IP litigation and enforcement costs, licensing and injunction risks, limits of protection across countries, and theft or employee departures. It also introduces extensive, changing data privacy and security obligations and their potential effects on reputation, customers, products, and legal exposure.

nodes.title: AI Responsibility and Intellectual Property Risks
key_items: Issues relating to the responsible use of our technologies, including AI in our offerings, may result in reputational or financial harm and liability.

Actions to adequately protect our IP rights could result in substantial costs to us and our ability to compete could be harmed if we are unsuccessful or if we are prohibited from making or selling our products.
nodes.summary: The page warns that sustainability-related expectations and compliance may raise costs, affect customer relationships, and harm reputation or expose the company to liability. Responsible use and regulation of AI may create legal, ethical, reputational, competitive, operational, and financial risks, increase compliance and development costs, and slow adoption. IP disputes and protection efforts may be costly and lead to damages, licensing payments, countersuits, or restrictions on products. Patent, trademark, trade-secret, contractual, and legal protections may be inadequate, especially abroad, risking theft, weaker competitiveness, and uncertain protection of innovations.

nodes.title: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws, rules, regulations and other obligations. These areas could damage our reputation, deter current and potential customers, affect our product design, or result in legal or regulatory proceedings and liability.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from evolving privacy, cybersecurity, AI, and data-transfer laws worldwide, including fines, litigation, operational changes, restrictions on data use, reputational harm, and failures by the company or its partners to comply with legal, contractual, or stated privacy commitments. It also warns that tax audits, changing laws, rates, deductions, and other factors may increase liabilities or effective taxes and hurt results. Litigation and investigations may be costly or lead to damages, fines, injunctions, or other remedies. Finally, substantial notes and a commercial-paper program create repayment, refinancing, covenant, cash-flow, flexibility, and financing risks.

nodes.title: Privacy, Tax, and Legal Risks
key_items: We may have exposure to additional tax liabilities and our operating results may be adversely impacted by changes in tax laws, higher than expected tax rates and other tax-related factors.
Our business is exposed to the risks associated with litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings.
nodes.summary: Changing data-protection laws may require business and technology changes; noncompliance could trigger enforcement, litigation, restrictions, and reputational or financial harm. Tax audits, legal changes, shifting tax rates and incentives, international tax rules, and other factors may increase liabilities or effective rates and hurt results and cash flows. Ongoing and future litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings—including a securities class action—could cause fines, damages, injunctions, costly disruptions, or other material adverse effects.

nodes.title: Our indebtedness could adversely affect our financial position and cash flows from operations, and prevent us from implementing our strategy or fulfilling our contractual obligations.
nodes.summary: The company’s $9.7 billion in notes due through 2060 and $575 million commercial paper program may strain cash flows and hinder strategy or contractual performance. Notes must be repaid or refinanced at maturity; refinancing may be unavailable or on worse terms. Debt and contractual restrictions could divert cash to debt service, increase economic and competitive vulnerability, limit business flexibility and future financing, and restrict liens, mergers, asset sales, or business changes. Uncontrollable events could cause covenant breaches; without waivers, debt may become immediately payable. Credit-rating changes could reduce securities’ value and liquidity and impair or worsen future financing.

nodes.title: Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws and agreement with Microsoft could delay or prevent a change in control.
nodes.summary: Delaware law, NVIDIA’s charter and bylaws, and its Microsoft Xbox agreement may delay or prevent a change in control. Anti-takeover provisions include board authority to issue preferred stock, change its size, and amend bylaws; restrictions on shareholder written consent and special meetings; advance notice rules for nominations and proposals; and supermajority amendment requirements. If an offer targets at least 30% of common stock, Microsoft may have first and last rights of refusal. These measures may deter acquisitions and proxy contests, limit shareholders’ choice of directors, and impede desired corporate actions.

summary: The section describes risks that could harm NVIDIA’s business, financial condition, results, reputation, and stock price. These include rapid technological and market change; competition and uncertain product adoption; demand-forecasting, supply-chain, manufacturing, quality, and product-defect risks; economic, international, geopolitical, climate, and business disruptions; cybersecurity, privacy, data, and system-control risks; reliance on customers, partners, suppliers, employees, and infrastructure; acquisitions and investments; fluctuating results; regulation, export controls, sustainability, responsible AI, intellectual property, taxes, litigation, and debt; and legal provisions that may impede a change in control.

title: Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments
key_items: Item 1C. Cybersecurity Risk management and strategy; Governance
Item 1C. Cybersecurity Risk management and strategy
summary: Item 1B reports no unresolved staff comments. Item 1C describes cybersecurity risk management aligned generally with ISO 27001, supported by evolving controls, external expert advice, integration with enterprise risk processes, and privacy and security training and policies. Vendor questionnaires and reviews assess third-party controls and high-risk suppliers’ standards and security requirements. Further risks are referenced in Item 1A. The Board oversees information security; the Audit Committee reviews policies, practices, and controls and receives regular updates, while the Board receives annual reports. Executive and cross-functional teams review threats, refine practices, and help direct incident response. A Chief Security Officer, with over 17 years of government and private-sector experience, reports to the SVP of Software Engineering and manages material cybersecurity risks.

title: Properties, Legal Proceedings, and Mine Safety
summary: The company’s headquarters are in Santa Clara, California, with approximately 3 million square feet of owned and leased office and building space. It also leases local data center space and owns or leases data center, R&D, sales, and administrative facilities across the U.S. and internationally, mainly in China, India, Israel, and Taiwan. Facilities are considered suitable; assets are not allocated by segment. Lease obligations and legal proceedings are discussed in referenced financial-statement notes. Mine safety disclosures are not applicable. The page begins Part II.

title: Item 5. Market for Registrant's Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
summary: NVIDIA common stock trades on Nasdaq under NVDA, with public trading beginning in 1999 and approximately 382 registered shareholders as of February 16, 2024. The text details the expanded, non-expiring repurchase authorization; fiscal 2024 buybacks, remaining authorization, quarterly repurchases, and subsequent purchases; buyback methods and the program’s discretionary nature; cash dividends and their board approval condition; and shares withheld for RSU taxes. It also describes a five-year total-return comparison with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, including methodology, source, and annual index values.

title: Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations

nodes.title: NVIDIA Overview and Supply Challenges
nodes.summary: Introduces the financial discussion and advises readers to consider the report’s risk factors, financial statements, and other cautions. Describes NVIDIA’s accelerated-computing platforms, two operating segments, and corporate history. Reviews surging data-center demand, supply expansion and commitments, and risks from capacity constraints or excess inventory. Explains the complexity of frequent product transitions, potential effects on revenue, costs, quality, and customer deployments, and uncertainty in demand and monetization for emerging applications such as DGX Cloud, Omniverse, large language models, and generative AI.

nodes.title: Trade Controls, Economic Factors, and Israel Conflict
nodes.summary: The page describes U.S. export licensing restrictions on advanced chips and systems, their effects on China sales and competition, efforts to offer alternatives, and risks to future sales and supply-chain flexibility. It outlines how inflation, interest rates, volatility, supply constraints, and geopolitical conditions may affect demand, costs, and operations. It also reports monitoring the Israel-Hamas conflict’s effects on regional employees, development, operations, and revenue; impacts have so far been limited, but prolonged conflict could cause disruption.

nodes.title: Fiscal Year 2024 Summary
nodes.summary: Fiscal 2024 revenue was $60.9 billion, up 126%, with gross margin rising 15.8 percentage points to 72.7%; operating expenses were up 2%, while operating income, net income, and diluted earnings per share rose 681%, 581%, and 586%, respectively. NVIDIA describes its accelerated-computing platforms and four markets: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. Data Center revenue grew 217% (compute 244%, networking 133%) on broad AI-infrastructure demand; Gaming rose 15% as channel inventory normalized and demand grew; Professional Visualization rose 1%; Automotive rose 21%, mainly from self-driving platforms. Higher gross margin reflected Data Center growth and lower inventory provisions relative to revenue. Operating expenses grew with staffing and compensation; fiscal 2023 included a $1.4 billion charge for terminating the proposed Arm acquisition.

nodes.title: Market Platform Highlights
nodes.summary: NVIDIA reported fiscal 2024 revenue growth across Data Center ($47.5B, +217%), Gaming ($10.4B, +15%), Professional Visualization ($1.6B, +1%) and Automotive ($1.1B, +21%). Data Center highlights included AI inference platforms and services, an estimated 40% of revenue from inference, cloud-provider demand, expected automotive processing growth, and Spectrum-X networking. Gaming launches included RTX GPUs, AI and ray-tracing features, and a milestone of 500 RTX games and applications. Professional Visualization introduced RTX Ada GPUs and Omniverse Cloud. Automotive announcements covered a MediaTek chip partnership, Foxconn EV collaboration, and DRIVE adoption by six automakers.

summary: Reviews NVIDIA’s financial performance, business platforms, supply and product-transition challenges, and risks from export controls, economic conditions, and geopolitical events. Reports fiscal 2024 revenue of $60.9 billion, up 126%, with higher margins and sharp increases in operating income, net income, and earnings per share. Summarizes results and developments across Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive, including AI infrastructure and inference, GPUs and ray tracing, Omniverse, networking, and automotive partnerships and adoption.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
key_items: Revenue Recognition Revenue Allowances; License and Development Arrangements; Contracts with Multiple Performance Obligations; Change in Accounting Estimate
summary: The company’s U.S. GAAP statements rely on estimates, with critical estimates involving inventory, income taxes, and revenue recognition. Tax estimates cover deferred taxes, contingencies, valuation allowances ($1.6 billion in 2024; $1.5 billion in 2023), and uncertain tax positions. Revenue estimates address returns, customer rebates and incentives, development-project progress, and identifying and allocating transaction prices among performance obligations. Longer estimated equipment lives increased 2024 operating income by $135 million and net income by $114 million ($0.05 per share).

The page defines gross profit and cost of revenue, reports gross margin rising to 72.7% from 56.9% on Data Center growth and lower inventory provisions, and details inventory provisions and releases. Operating expenses rose 2% to $11.329 billion, mainly from employee compensation, while R&D and sales and administrative costs increased and the 2023 $1.4 billion Arm termination cost was written off.

Also discusses forthcoming OECD Pillar Two minimum-tax rules, their expected near-term impact, and related financial-statement notes.

Defines cost of revenue and gross profit, explains higher gross margins and inventory provisions or releases, and details operating expenses, including the Arm termination charge. Also reports other income and expenses, taxes, effective rates, IRS audit benefits, factors affecting tax rates, and expected effects of OECD Pillar Two rules.

nodes.title: Note 1 - Organization and Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Organization and Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s policy note describes its corporate history and terminology, 52- or 53-week fiscal year, consolidation of wholly owned subsidiaries, and use and ongoing review of estimates under U.S. GAAP. It details a 2023 extension of certain equipment useful lives and its financial impact. Revenue recognition follows the five-step contract process and covers product, licensing, development, and cloud revenue. Product revenue is recognized on transfer of control, with service revenue recognized over time; returns, taxes, rebates, and marketing funds reduce revenue and are estimated and accrued.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The notes describe revenue accounting for customized license and development arrangements, software licenses and support, cloud subscriptions and usage, and contracts with multiple performance obligations, including cost-based progress, timing, and standalone-price allocation. They cover warranty terms and accruals; valuation, expense recognition, and forfeiture estimates for RSUs, PSUs, market-based PSUs, and ESPP awards; and the range and uncertainty of ongoing or potential litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
key_items: Foreign Currency Remeasurement; Income Taxes; Net Income Per Share; Cash and Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities
Cash and Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities
nodes.summary: The notes describe litigation accounting: probable, estimable losses are accrued under U.S. GAAP, though actual liabilities may differ. Foreign-currency monetary items are remeasured at period-end rates, nonmonetary items at historical rates, and resulting gains or losses enter earnings. Income-tax policies cover current and deferred taxes, valuation allowances, uncertain tax positions, and related interest and penalties; a $1.6 billion allowance existed at January 28, 2024. Basic and diluted EPS methods are explained. Cash equivalents, marketable securities, available-for-sale debt accounting, realized gains and losses, and impairment reviews are also described.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
key_items: Fair Value of Financial Instruments; Concentration of Credit Risk; Inventories; Property and Equipment; Leases
nodes.summary: The notes describe accounting policies for financial instruments, credit risk, inventory, property and equipment, and leases. Securities are measured at fair value, with gains and losses treated according to security or derivative classification and hedge designation; credit allowances and write-downs enter other income or expense. Credit risk is managed through investment limits, customer reviews, and loss allowances. Inventory is costed on an adjusted standard basis and written down for excess, obsolescence, or commitments. Property is depreciated or amortized over estimated useful lives, with disposal gains or losses recorded. Operating leases are recognized using discounted payments, qualifying extension or termination options, and straight-line expense; lease and non-lease components are combined.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
key_items: Goodwill; Intangible Assets and Other Long-Lived Assets; Business Combination; Investments in Non-Affiliated Entities
Intangible Assets and Other Long-Lived Assets
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes accounting policies for goodwill impairment testing annually or when indicated, using qualitative factors or income and market valuation analyses. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized over one to twenty years; long-lived assets are tested for impairment when circumstances warrant, with disposal assets measured at the lower of carrying value or fair value less selling costs. Acquisitions allocate purchase price to assets and liabilities, with residual goodwill; estimates may be adjusted during a one-year measurement period, while acquisition costs are expensed. Public equity investments are fair-valued; private investments use the measurement alternative and are assessed for impairment, with gains, losses, and impairment charges reported in other income or expense.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
key_items: Recent Accounting Pronouncements Not Yet Adopted
nodes.summary: The notes describe two FASB standards not yet adopted. A November 2023 standard requires additional disclosures of significant operating-segment expenses, applies retrospectively to fiscal 2025 annual and fiscal 2026 interim reporting, and is under evaluation. A December 2023 standard changes income tax disclosures, including rate-reconciliation and taxes-paid details; it applies to annual periods beginning after December 15, 2024, permits early adoption and retrospective application, and is expected to be adopted in fiscal 2026. Its impact is also being evaluated.

The note outlines NVIDIA’s corporate history, fiscal year, consolidation, estimates, and 2023 useful-life change. It explains revenue recognition across products, services, licenses, development, cloud, and multi-obligation contracts, plus returns, warranties, and stock-based compensation. Other policies cover litigation, foreign currency, income taxes, EPS, cash and securities, financial instruments and credit risk, inventory, property, leases, goodwill, intangible and long-lived assets, acquisitions, and equity investments. It also describes two pending FASB standards on segment and income-tax disclosures, their timelines, and evaluation.

nodes.title: Note 2 - Business Combination
key_items: Termination of the Arm Share Purchase Agreement
nodes.summary: In February 2022, NVIDIA and SoftBank terminated their agreement for NVIDIA to acquire Arm because of significant regulatory challenges. NVIDIA recorded a $1.4 billion acquisition termination cost in fiscal 2023, writing off the prepayment made when the agreement was signed.

nodes.title: Note 3 - Leases
key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s operating leases cover headquarters, domestic and international offices, and data centers, generally expiring in fiscal 2025–2035. At January 28, 2024, future minimum payments totaled $1.539 billion; after $192 million imputed interest, present value was $1.347 billion, including $228 million short-term and $1.119 billion long-term liabilities. Additional data-center leases totaling $1.1 billion are expected to begin in fiscal 2025, with 1–10-year terms. Lease expense was $269 million in 2024, $193 million in 2023, and $168 million in 2022; short-term and variable expenses were not significant. Supplemental disclosures report operating lease cash flows and assets obtained in exchange for obligations for 2024–2022. Weighted-average remaining terms and discount rates were 6.1 years and 3.76% in 2024, versus 6.8 years and 3.21% in 2023.

nodes.title: Note 4 - Stock-Based Compensation
key_items: Year Ended Jan 29, 2023; RSUs, PSUs and Market-based PSUs
nodes.summary: Note 4 describes stock-based compensation from RSUs, performance-based and market-based PSUs, and the ESPP. It reports compensation expense by income-statement category for fiscal 2024, 2023, and 2022, noting amounts capitalized in inventory were insignificant. It summarizes equity awards granted and ESPP shares purchased, including grant-date fair values and per-share prices. At January 28, 2024, $8.6 billion of unearned compensation remained, expected to be recognized over weighted-average periods of 2.5 years for RSUs and PSUs and 0.8 years for ESPP.

summary: The section presents NVIDIA’s consolidated cash flows for fiscal 2022–2024, including operating, investing, and financing activities, changes in cash, balances, and supplemental tax and interest payments. The accompanying notes cover significant accounting policies and pending standards; termination of the Arm acquisition; operating lease commitments, expenses, and metrics; and stock-based compensation plans, expenses, awards, and unearned compensation.

It also reconciles basic and diluted net income per share for three fiscal years, showing net income, weighted-average shares, the dilutive impact of equity awards, per-share results, and awards excluded as anti-dilutive, with calculation definitions.

key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: Goodwill totaled $4.4 billion at January 28, 2024 ($4.1 billion in Compute & Networking and $370 million in Graphics), versus $4.4 billion at January 29, 2023 ($4.0 billion and $370 million, respectively). A $59 million increase in fiscal 2024 from an immaterial acquisition was allocated to Compute & Networking. Annual qualitative impairment tests in the fourth quarters of fiscal 2024, 2023, and 2022 found no impairment.

nodes.title: Note 7 - Amortizable Intangible Assets
key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: Note 7 reports amortizable intangible assets by category—acquisition-related assets and patents/licensed technology—with gross, accumulated amortization, and net carrying amounts at January 28, 2024 and January 29, 2023. It notes that amortization began in fiscal 2023 on a $630 million Mellanox in-process R&D asset. Amortization expense was $614 million, $699 million, and $563 million in fiscal 2024, 2023, and 2022. Estimated future amortization of the January 2024 net balance totals $1.112 billion, including $555 million, $261 million, $150 million, $37 million, and $9 million in successive fiscal-year periods, plus $100 million in 2030 and thereafter.

nodes.title: Note 8 - Cash Equivalents and Marketable Securities
nodes.summary: Note 8 summarizes NVIDIA’s available-for-sale cash equivalents and marketable debt securities by investment type, amortized cost, unrealized gains and losses, estimated fair value, and balance-sheet classification for Jan. 28, 2024 and Jan. 29, 2023. It details securities in continuous unrealized-loss positions by category and duration, noting losses mainly reflect interest-rate changes and realized gains or losses were insignificant. It also presents amortized cost and fair value by contractual maturity: under one year and one to five years.

nodes.title: Note 9 - Fair Value of Financial Assets and Liabilities and Investments in Non-Affiliated Entities
key_items: Assets; Liabilities (1); Investments in Non-Affiliated Entities
NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The note explains that fair values use quoted prices for identical or similar assets, with hierarchy classifications reviewed quarterly. It lists Level 1 and Level 2 classifications for cash equivalents, marketable securities, publicly traded equity investments, and notes payable; debt liabilities are carried at issuance value less unamortized discounts and costs. Investments in non-affiliated entities include publicly traded securities measured at fair value and private-company securities measured under the measurement alternative. Marketable holdings were $225 million and $11 million in 2024 and 2023, with insignificant gains or losses. Non-marketable holdings rose from $288 million to $1.321 billion through $859 million in additions, $194 million in unrealized gains, and $20 million in impairments or losses. A private-company secondary offering generated a $178 million unrealized gain; 2024 unrealized gains on holdings still owned were $174 million. Cumulative unrealized gains were $270 million and losses and impairments $45 million; 2023 and 2022 gains and losses were insignificant.

key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
Accrued and Other Current Liabilities:; Other Long-Term Liabilities:
nodes.summary: Note 10 reports customer concentrations in accounts receivable for 2024 and 2023; inventory categories and totals, plus inventory provisions charged to cost of revenue; property and equipment balances, useful-life and depreciation/amortization details, and assets acquired by assuming liabilities; and other assets, including additional short-term prepaid supply agreements. It lists accrued current and other long-term liabilities, explaining excess inventory obligations, deferred revenue, and income tax payable. It also reconciles deferred revenue for 2024 and 2023, reports revenue recognized from prior-period balances, and describes remaining performance obligations.

nodes.title: Deferred Revenue
nodes.summary: The text details NVIDIA’s accrued and other current liabilities and other long-term liabilities at January 28, 2024, and January 29, 2023, with category balances and totals. It notes inventory-obligation expenses of about $1.4 billion and $1.1 billion, explains deferred revenue and long-term income tax payable, and presents deferred revenue additions, recognized revenue, and opening and closing balances for fiscal 2024 and 2023. It also reports revenue recognized from prior-period deferred balances and $1.1 billion in remaining performance obligations, expected to be recognized about 40% within twelve months and the rest later, excluding obligations on contracts of one year or less.

nodes.title: Note 11 - Derivative Financial Instruments
nodes.summary: NVIDIA uses foreign currency forward contracts as cash flow hedges for operating expenses, deferring gains or losses in accumulated other comprehensive income until the expenses are recognized or hedge ineffectiveness occurs. Non-designated forwards offset currency-related fair-value changes in monetary assets and liabilities through other income or expense. Notional values at January 28, 2024 and January 29, 2023 were $1,168 million and $1,128 million for designated contracts, and $597 million and $366 million for non-designated contracts. Fair values were not significant; designated contracts mature within 18 months, expected next-year deferred gains or losses were not significant, and fiscal 2024 and 2023 hedge effects on other comprehensive income were not significant, with all designated instruments highly effective.

nodes.title: Note 12 - Debt
nodes.summary: Note 12 details long-term debt at January 28, 2024 and January 29, 2023, including note maturities, remaining terms, effective interest rates, carrying values, unamortized discounts and issuance costs, and short- versus long-term portions. The 0.309% notes due 2023 were repaid in fiscal 2024. Notes are unsecured senior obligations, effectively subordinated to subsidiary liabilities, pay interest semiannually, and may be redeemed before maturity with a make-whole premium. The company met its non-financial covenants. Its $575 million commercial paper program supports general corporate purposes; none was outstanding at January 28, 2024.

nodes.title: Note 13 - Commitments and Contingencies
Purchase Obligations
nodes.summary: Note 13 describes purchase obligations for product components, supply and capacity agreements, software and technology licenses, other goods and services, and long-lived assets. As of January 28, 2024, inventory purchase and long-term supply and capacity obligations totaled $16.1 billion. Contract manufacturers may procure inventory under company-defined criteria; before firm orders, the company may cancel, reschedule, or adjust requirements, but may owe costs incurred. Other purchase obligations totaled $4.6 billion, including $3.5 billion in multi-year cloud service agreements, primarily for research and development.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
key_items: Fiscal Year:; Accrual for Product Warranty Liabilities; Jan 28, 2024; Litigation Securities Class Action and Derivative Lawsuits
Litigation Securities Class Action and Derivative Lawsuits
nodes.summary: The notes report $20.707 billion in future purchase commitments as of January 28, 2024, mainly due in fiscal 2025, and product warranty liabilities of $306 million, up from $82 million a year earlier. Warranty additions and utilization are detailed for fiscal 2022–2024; recent additions primarily related to Compute & Networking. NVIDIA describes various indemnities, whose maximum exposure cannot be estimated, and has accrued no liability. The securities class action alleging misleading statements about channel inventory and cryptocurrency-related GPU demand was dismissed in 2021; the Ninth Circuit partly reversed that dismissal in 2023, denied rehearing, and NVIDIA sought a stay while pursuing Supreme Court review.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The text describes NVIDIA-related derivative lawsuits alleging fiduciary-duty and securities-law violations over statements about channel inventory and cryptocurrency mining’s effect on GPU demand. Several cases remain stayed pending resolution of the securities litigation appeal; parties are discussing next steps, and one additional Delaware action is also stayed. Plaintiffs seek unspecified damages and remedies including disgorgement and governance reforms. As of January 28, 2024, NVIDIA recorded no loss accrual because liabilities were possible but not probable, and losses could not generally be estimated; it does not expect other ordinary-course legal actions to materially harm its financial condition or results.

The note covers $20.707 billion in future purchase commitments, including $16.1 billion for inventory, supply and capacity and $4.6 billion for other goods and services, largely multi-year cloud agreements; cancellation before firm orders may still incur costs. It details warranty liabilities and activity, describes indemnities with unestimable maximum exposure and no accrual, and reviews securities and derivative litigation concerning disclosures about channel inventory and cryptocurrency-related GPU demand, including case status, claimed remedies, lack of loss accrual, and management’s assessment of other legal actions.

nodes.title: Note 14 - Income Taxes
key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: Note 14 reports NVIDIA’s income taxes for fiscal 2022–2024: current and deferred federal, state, and foreign taxes; U.S. and foreign pretax income; and reconciliation of tax expense to the 21% federal statutory rate, including state taxes, foreign-derived income, stock compensation, foreign-rate differences, credits, acquisition termination costs, IP domestication, and other items. It details deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances, indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings, tax-loss and credit carryforwards and expirations, and potential limits on their use. It also reconciles unrecognized tax benefits, explains their classification and related interest and penalties, discusses estimation uncertainty, and identifies jurisdictions subject to examination and current audits.

nodes.title: Note 15 - Shareholders’ Equity
key_items: NVIDIA Corporation and Subsidiaries Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.summary: In August 2023, the board expanded NVIDIA’s share repurchase authorization by $25 billion, with no expiration. The company repurchased 21 million shares for $9.7 billion in fiscal 2024 and had $22.5 billion remaining authorization as of January 28, 2024; it later repurchased 2.8 million shares for $1.9 billion under a Rule 10b5-1 plan. Repurchases primarily offset employee-share dilution, with future activity dependent on market conditions and investment opportunities. Cash dividends totaled $395 million, $398 million, and $399 million in fiscal 2024, 2023, and 2022, respectively, subject to ongoing board approval. In fiscal 2022, 349 million treasury shares were retired and became authorized, unissued shares; repurchase-price excess reduced additional paid-in capital by $20 million and retained earnings by $12 billion. The text also introduces NVIDIA’s Compensation Recovery Policy, last updated November 30, 2023.

title: Policy Purpose | Applicability
summary: The policy authorizes recovery of certain compensation following an Accounting Restatement and applies to Incentive Compensation received on or after the Effective Date when the officer meets specified service, performance-period, listed-securities, and Lookback Period conditions. It is designed to comply with the Compensation Recovery Rules and binds Covered Officers and, where required, their legal representatives and beneficiaries. It replaces the Prior Policy for compensation received on or after the Effective Date; the Prior Policy remains applicable to earlier compensation.

title: Policy Statement | Responsibilities
summary: The policy requires prompt, fault-independent recovery of incentive compensation affected by accounting restatements, including related notional-account contributions and earnings; stock-price/TSR impacts may use a documented reasonable estimate. Recovery exceptions apply only when specified enforcement costs or qualified-plan risks make recovery impracticable, subject to committee approval and documented reasonable recovery efforts where required. The Committee chooses lawful recovery methods and timing, and the Company makes required disclosures. Officers receive no indemnity or expense advancement for recovery, while other Company remedies remain available; prior recoveries are credited, and recovery is not grounds for constructive termination or breach claims. Noncompliance may cause delisting. The policy sets administration, decision-making, delegation, liability protection, severability, and amendment or termination rules.

title: Speak Up | Reporting Concerns
summary: Anyone aware of a possible Policy violation must report it to their supervisor, Corporate Legal, or NVIDIA-Compliance, or anonymously through EthicsPoint by U.S. phone or web. Identifying oneself is encouraged to enable follow-up and investigation. NVIDIA will protect confidentiality and prohibit retaliation against good-faith reporters or investigation cooperators, even if allegations are unsubstantiated.

title: Resources | Questions
summary: The policy directs questions to Corporate Legal and defines key terms: Accounting Restatement and the date it is required or ordered; the Board, Committee, Company, applicable recovery rules, Covered Officer, and October 2, 2023 effective date; Exchange Act, SEC, Nasdaq Rule 5608, and TSR; Financial Reporting Measures and Incentive Compensation; the three-year-plus-transition-period Lookback Period, excluding years before the effective date; the prior April 1, 2009 policy; when compensation is considered received; and Recoverable Incentive Compensation, calculated as excess incentive pay during the Lookback Period based on restated results, before taxes and deductions.
